opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it in terms of what we already did for vision and hearing. For those senses, we have a map: color has red, green, and blue, and sound has frequency and amplitude. That map lets you digitize a sensation, store it, transmit it, and reproduce it. Smell has never had that. We don't have a principled way to go from a molecule's structure to what it smells like, and we can't easily go backward from a desired scent to the molecules that would produce it.

So the path, as I see it, has a few steps. First is **reading**: building a map of odor space, so that given a molecule you can predict how a person would describe it, whether that's fruity, smoky, grassy, or musky. That's where machine learning comes in. Molecules are naturally graphs, atoms connected by bonds, so graph neural networks are a good fit. If you train them on carefully collected human perceptual data, you can learn an embedding where molecules that smell alike sit close together, even when they look structurally quite different. That's always been the puzzle of olfaction. Small changes to a molecule can completely change its smell, and very different molecules can smell nearly identical.

The second step is **sensing**: hardware that can detect what's in the air, at the sensitivity and specificity that matter, and then use that map to interpret it. Biology is wildly good at this. We have hundreds of different receptor types, and dogs have even more, so there's a lot to learn from how nature does combinatorial coding.

The third step is **writing**: actually generating or reproducing a scent on demand, the way a printer or a speaker reproduces images or sound.

None of this works without good data, and that's been one of the biggest bottlenecks. Human olfactory data is noisy, people describe smells differently, and the field just hasn't had the large, clean datasets that vision had with ImageNet. A lot of the work is unglamorous: training panels of people to rate odors consistently and building that foundation.

The reason it matters goes well beyond perfume. Smell is chemistry, and chemistry carries information about disease, food spoilage, safety, and the environment. Insects find us by smell, so better repellents are on the table too. If we can give computers a real sense of smell, we open up a whole channel of information about the world that we've mostly been ignoring.

r001.rationale: The response includes a writing step: generating or reproducing a scent on demand.

r002.rationale: It discusses graph neural networks and sensing hardware, but does not identify a foundation model as necessary for scent detection.

r003.rationale: It says clean human olfactory data is a bottleneck, but does not connect insufficient data to building a foundation model for smell.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that smell is really the last of the senses to be digitized. We did it for vision with cameras, for hearing with microphones, and in both of those cases the physics was relatively tractable. Light is a wave, you can characterize it by wavelength and intensity. Sound is a wave too. Smell is different. It's a chemical sense, and the space of possible molecules is enormous, something on the order of ten to the sixtieth or more plausible small molecules. So there's no single "wavelength" of smell. The relationship between a molecule's structure and how it smells has been one of the great unsolved problems in neuroscience and chemistry for a long time.

So the path, as I see it, breaks into a few pieces. The first is the map. Before you can build a camera, it helps to have a color space, something like RGB, that tells you how to represent the thing you're sensing. For smell we didn't have that. That was a lot of the work we did early on, first at Google Research and then at Osmo, training graph neural networks on molecular structure to predict human odor descriptors. And the surprising thing was that it worked. We got to the point where the model's predictions were about as close to the panel average as any individual trained human panelist. And when we looked at the learned embedding, it turned out to be a kind of principal odor map where molecules that smell alike sit near each other, even when their chemical structures look nothing alike.

The second piece is the sensor side, actually reading molecules out of the air. That's genuinely hard. Biology does it with hundreds of receptor types working in parallel, and a mass spectrometer or gas chromatograph is big and slow and expensive. So part of the path is bringing chemical sensing hardware down in cost and size, and using the map to interpret what those sensors see.

And the third piece, which I think people underestimate, is the write side, not just reading smell but reproducing it. If you can detect a scent, decompose it into its constituent molecules, and then reconstruct it somewhere else, that's teleporting scent, the same way we send images and sound across the internet today. We've actually done early versions of that, taking a fresh plum, reading it out, and printing a formula that smells like the plum.

So I think of the whole thing as a stack. Map, read, write. And the reason I'm optimistic is that the map, which was the piece that seemed hopelessly complex for decades, turned out to be learnable from data. Once you have that, the other pieces become engineering problems. Hard engineering problems, but engineering problems. And the payoff is huge, in health, where diseases have characteristic smells long before other symptoms, in food, in safety, and frankly in just preserving things that matter to people. Smells are tied to memory in a way nothing else is, and right now we have no way to save them.

r001.rationale: The response includes a “write side” for reproducing smells and describes reading a plum and printing a formula that smells like it.

r002.rationale: It describes a learned odor map and using that map to interpret sensors, but does not identify building a foundation model as necessary for scent detection.

r003.rationale: It does not identify insufficient data as a missing prerequisite for building a foundation model for smell.

astra-6.text:
I think the path starts with making smell computable. With vision, we have pixels, and with sound, we have waveforms—representations that let us capture something in the world and give it to a machine. With smell, even deciding what that representation should be is a big part of the problem.

You have molecules on one side and a perceptual experience on the other. How do you get from the structure of a molecule to whether it smells floral, grassy, or smoky? It’s not a simple lookup table, and molecules that look similar can smell very different. But that’s a problem we can start to tackle with machine learning: learn a representation that connects chemistry to perception and then see whether it generalizes to molecules we haven’t measured before.

That’s one piece of giving computers a sense of smell. You also need to sample the physical world and detect what’s there. And everyday smells are mixtures, so predicting the smell of an individual molecule doesn’t solve the whole thing. But if we can build a useful bridge between molecules and perception, we have a foundation for interpreting what a sensor detects—and eventually for recording and reproducing smells.

r001.rationale: The response includes eventually recording and reproducing smells, which communicates generating smells as part of the goal.

r002.rationale: It describes a molecule-to-perception bridge as a foundation for interpreting sensor detections, but does not identify building a foundation model as necessary for scent detection.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify insufficient data as a missing prerequisite for building a foundation model for smell.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is to recognize that smell is fundamentally a different kind of problem from vision or hearing. With a camera or a microphone, we have a pretty clear idea of what to measure: light or pressure waves. With smell, you’re dealing with molecules, and the relationship between a molecule’s structure and what it smells like is surprisingly hard to predict.

So one of the foundational questions is: Can we build a map of smell? Can we take a molecular structure and place it somewhere in a space where nearby molecules smell similar, even if their structures look quite different? Machine learning gives us a way to start learning that relationship.

But that’s one piece of giving a computer a sense of smell. You also need to sample the physical world, detect what molecules are present, and connect those measurements to perception. And real-world smells are mixtures, which makes the problem much richer. I think the path is to build those pieces together: a way to capture smells, a representation that lets us reason about them, and eventually a way to reproduce them.

r001.rationale: The response includes eventually reproducing smells as part of giving computers a sense of smell.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning a representation of smell, but does not identify building a foundation model as necessary for scent detection.

r003.rationale: It does not identify insufficient data as a missing prerequisite for building a foundation model for smell.
